anatomy.lede: A ribbon eel is almost all length: a whip-thin moray with a frilled snout, built to slip into narrow burrows and peer out at passing fish.

hotspots.label: Flared nostril
hotspots.text: The front nostrils are long tubes that end in fan-like expansions, flaring from the tip of the snout like small leaves.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Its retina differs markedly in structure from those of three other morays studied, a difference researchers link to its shallow, sunlit home.

hotspots.label: Chin tentacles
hotspots.text: Three small fleshy tentacles sit at the tip of the lower jaw, with a single pointed projection at the tip of the snout.

hotspots.label: Blue phase
hotspots.text: Bright blue with a yellow snout and jaw is the colour usually described for males. Juveniles are black, and the largest animals turn yellow.

hotspots.label: Dorsal fin
hotspots.text: A high, yellow dorsal fin runs along the back. Like the anal fin, it has no spines.

body.lede: Inside, the ribbon eel is as unusual as it looks outside.

systems.title: A spine of hundreds of bones
systems.text: Its backbone has 270 to 286 vertebrae, which is what makes such a long, thin, flexible body possible.

systems.title: Organs behind the vent
systems.text: In ribbon eels the reproductive organs lie behind the anus rather than in front of it, as in other fishes. A 1990 study described Rhinomuraena as the first vertebrate genus known with this arrangement.

systems.title: Eyes for bright water
systems.text: Comparing two shallow-water and two deep-sea morays, researchers found that the light sensitivity of each species' eye cells closely matched the light in its habitat, with the ribbon eel's retina standing apart in structure.

survival.lede: A slender fish on an open reef survives by staying close to cover.

tactics.title: Never far from home
tactics.text: It lives in burrows in sand or rubble beside coral reefs, in lagoons and on seaward reefs, and rarely leaves them.

tactics.title: Only the head shows
tactics.text: Secretive by nature, it usually stays hidden with just its head out, waiting for small fishes to come within reach.

tactics.title: Larvae seeking shelter
tactics.text: Large moray larvae, probably of this species, have been filmed swimming near the bottom in shallow water and trying to enter small crevices — perhaps looking for a safe place to change into juvenile eels.

threats.title: Collected for aquariums
threats.text: It is caught commercially for the aquarium trade. FishBase rates its vulnerability to fishing as high to very high and its resilience as very low, with populations estimated to need more than 14 years to double.

life.lede: A ribbon eel's life is told in colours, though what each colour means is still being worked out.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: In 2014, fertilised ribbon eel eggs laid at the Vienna Zoo hatched into feeding larvae for the first time anywhere, and the larvae were kept alive for seven days.

stages.name: Leptocephalus larva
stages.text: Like all eels it begins as a transparent, leaf-like larva. Large, greenish moray larvae seen off Indonesia are thought to be ribbon eels, but this has not been confirmed.

stages.name: Black juvenile
stages.text: Small juveniles are jet black with a yellow dorsal fin.

stages.name: Blue adult
stages.text: Adults turn bright blue with a yellow snout, lower jaw and dorsal fin, a phase usually interpreted as male.

stages.name: Yellow adult
stages.text: The largest animals turn yellow, a phase usually interpreted as female. But the Vienna Zoo study found that, in captivity, colour did not reflect an eel's sex or maturity, and sex change has not been confirmed.
